title: Three Generations of the Pataudi Women Took London — and Sara Ali Khan Made the Whole Internet Misty
excerpt: Sharmila Tagore, Amrita Singh and Sara in one frame, captioned 'Moments forever.' It's the softest flex in Bollywood right now, and the diaspora can't stop replaying it.
body:
There are red carpets that try this hard and fail. Then there's **Sara Ali Khan**, posting a fistful of grainy, golden-hour London snapshots and casually breaking the timeline with the most disarming thing a star can offer in 2026: an actual family that likes each other.

The caption was barely there — "London for a minute," then "Moments forever." Two lines. But the photographs did the talking, and what they showed was rare even by Bollywood's dynastic standards: three generations of Pataudi-Tagore women in a single getaway, away from cameras they didn't summon, in the city that has quietly become the family's second home.

There's Sara, all easy charm in the English summer light. There's her mother **Amrita Singh**, who has been a near-constant in her daughter's feed and a fierce presence at every premiere. And there, anchoring the frame, is **Sharmila Tagore** — the legend Sara fondly calls "Amma," the woman who was a screen icon before three of the people reading this were born, and who at 80-something still photographs like she's about to deliver a line that wins the scene.

https://x.com/abplive/status/2068895839599358367

> "London for a minute. Moments forever." — Sara Ali Khan, on Instagram

What makes the post hit isn't glamour, exactly — though there's plenty. It's the lineage. Sharmila Tagore was the face that defined a certain kind of Hindi cinema cool in the '60s and '70s; she married a cricketing prince, the Nawab of Pataudi, and became royalty twice over. Amrita Singh was the firebrand leading lady of the '80s. And Sara is the one who took the family name into the streaming era. To see all three in one candid carousel — no stylist, no step-and-repeat, just a holiday — is to watch six decades of Indian stardom collapse into a single phone screen.

The diaspora, predictably, lost it. For NRIs in London especially, the post landed like a love letter to their own city: the gardens, the grey-gold light, the unhurried walk that no Mumbai schedule ever allows. Sara has built a whole second persona as Bollywood's most enthusiastic traveller — spiritual retreats one week, mountain switchbacks the next, a beach somewhere in between — and her London diaries slot neatly into a feed that doubles as a wanderlust mood board for desis abroad. This particular trip, though, traded the usual solo-explorer energy for something warmer. It wasn't about the destination. It was about who she brought to it.

It also isn't the family's first London moment of the season. Sara and Sharmila Tagore were recently spotted at Pakistani actor **Kubra Khan's** birthday celebration in the city, and Sara had earlier shared a sweet theatre-outing photo with her mother and grandmother — a slow drip of updates that has turned the trio into the summer's most quietly watched travelogue. The English capital, with its old Pataudi ties and its enormous South Asian community, keeps pulling them back.

On the work front, Sara isn't coasting. She's gearing up for **Udta Teer**, a spy comedy that reunites her with **Ayushmann Khurrana** after *Pati Patni Aur Woh Do*, written and directed by Akash A Kaushik and backed by **Dharma Productions**. A spy comedy is exactly the register Sara does well — earnest, a little goofy, impossible to dislike — and pairing her again with Ayushmann is the kind of safe-bet chemistry studios print money on.

For now, though, the work can wait. The most-shared thing she's released this month isn't a trailer or a poster. It's a vacation. And in an industry that spends crores manufacturing the illusion of intimacy, there's something genuinely magnetic about a star who can stop the internet with three women, one city, and a caption she clearly didn't overthink. Diaspora viewers can find Sara's filmography — from *Kedarnath* to *Atrangi Re* — across **Netflix**, **Amazon Prime Video** and **Disney+ Hotstar** in the US, UK and Canada, but no algorithm is serving anything as warm as this. Some things you just have to scroll for.
